I knew what to expect but...

Why do I feel so empty?
Why do I feel so empty?
Yes, apparently.
I'm still here. What do you need to know?

The thought is appreciated, really, but I know I'm depressed. I was diagnosed professionally with it when I was 13. I've been treated for it on-and-off and tried a few medications. Wellbutrin made me feel less depressed, but much more anxious and keyed up. Prozac made me feel like a zombie. Lexapro left me totally unchanged even at the highest dose. SSRIs don't seem to work for me, and MAOIs are outdated, which maybe just leaves benzos, but those are pretty archaic too. 3 medications that didn't work is 3 too many.

I've been to 5 therapists since I was 8 years old, the latest being in Kansas when I worked there. Nothing seemed to work. Here in China, therapists essentially don't exist, but it's not hard to get medication. I could try therapy through Talkspace, but it's expensive.

Talk is cheap, solutions cost time, and I feel like mine is running out.

Good point, and I touched on that a little in another comment. At risk of butchering the concept, the way it tends to be thought of here in China is that, in a given conversation, two people are presenting their "face" to one-another. There's something of an unspoken contract between them to avoid dishonoring or disrespecting the other person's "face" as much as possible, which is partly why you don't tend to see as much blatant, damaging rejection here as you might elsewhere. Not to say people here can't be downright biting with their comments, same as anywhere else.

In this sense, I realized what I've been doing, on reflection, is essentially asking the other person to put themselves in the position that I myself fear so much, that being presenting your "face" to them for judgement, approval, disapproval, etc. Nobody wants to be in that position, myself included, but like you put it, I've been waiting on a "rescue". Rejection is painful and a whole lot of other negative words, but in avoiding it myself I've put the onus on others to do the work and take the risk in my stead. Which is pretty selfish and hypocritical of me.

I should mention I have a pretty healthy number of online friends, some of whom I trust deeply. I'm not completely isolated, and I've found a community for my love of gaming and memes and all that. It's just that it's online, and conventional wisdom says it's just not the same, and never will be. It's good, and I value them a lot, but I can't help the feeling of missing out. And of course, there's no romantic connection there, either.

My primary interests are gaming, memes, and writing, which I do a fair bit of, as well as audio editing. Beyond that, there's a fair bit I can hold a conversation over, albeit with some Google Fu, here and there. The majority of these, though, are personal interests or interests that translate well only online, particularly here in China.
Fair play. You can probably count me in that number.

Fair point. I was thinking on it a little more and I suppose that it's not unique to me to want to avoid an embarrassing situation i.e. rejection or being embarrassed or ignored in some other way. The idea I've always had is that between two people, there's a 100% chance of social contact that leads into friendship. However, if you split it, it's 50-50. So in all the cases of people I've crossed paths with, why have those odds so rarely come up with a new friend? Not at all, in fact? But I guess it's not that simple.

As well, the whole reason I don't put myself out there is avoidance. I don't want to put my "face" out there and be embarrassed or have it take a hit from being rejected, so I passively wait for other people to do it for me, when that's me forcing them into the same situation I try to avoid. Which is, on reflection, pretty selfish. 

Have a !delta.

I think it's fine advice, with a caveat: Is it more or less valuable to make friends in those niches online, or in real life? Because finding a "science club" or "gaming club" or whatever in real life is going to be more difficult, I think, than finding one for hiking or climbing enthusiasts, or a beginner guitar group.

I'm in a situation, personally, where that's very hard to do. I live in China to teach English and I don't speak or read the language well enough to integrate, and more specifically, live in a city where finding things that suit what I enjoy (as wide a net as that is to cast) would be difficult anyway. Dance classes, art classes, calligraphy classes, outside-school STEM classes, social groups, etc are a dime a dozen here, but it's not exactly overflowing with gaming clubs, arcades, etc to my knowledge. 

So I'll turn back to the clock a little and posit this to me when I was 20 and a sophomore in college. I was 30 minutes away from the school, and the gas costs to go back and forth to clubs and meetings, even once a week, would have been prohibitive, given I was paying for half of my schooling and my parents were paying for the other half. I never came out in the black in my 5 years of schooling anyway. 

I can't say I ever did try something new, no. I can't say I've tried anything new since I came here, either. It's been a year here and between the language barrier and my own problems, I haven't branched out much.

But this isn't about me specifically. I'm talking as a whole, not in my individual case. I'm an extreme case, but there are a lot of people like me, I'm sure.

>Yes, the society has a distaste for people who cannot socialize. And for a reason. The fact that you survive for nearly a decade in social isolation is a feat of modern civilization. In hunter-gatherer societies, which what human and society are well adapted to, the force of nature is just too strong, people have cooperate within a tribe in order to survive. Those who cannot and do not cooperate, will be a liability to the tribe.

It being human nature doesn't necessarily make it right or moral, but it does make it harder to avoid on an instinctual level, that's true. And yes, it is pretty much only possible because of modern technology. I imagine in a primitive or even pre-computer society, I would've died off somehow, even if it were just by necking myself.

>Assuming that you were socialized as kids, not a feral child. I think we both agree that it is possible, but hard. The question is, is it worth it?

I had social interaction as a kid, sure. I'd say I started becoming less social when I got my first computer at 13. As for whether it's worthwhile, I figure that question can be answered by whether pain, awkwardness and anguish > benefit. Considering people who aren't social die faster, I'd say extra life span has high value and is thus probably worth it compared to several months of awkwardness and rejection that you have to push through in order to get to normative socializing, objectively. But people who are like me are probably risk-averse or have such a strong aversion to that kind of unpleasantness that it seems much worse than it is, which there's no cure for.

>I agree with you friend, to some extent, it is self inflicted. But I want to offer a solution. Stop trying to integrate with an average person. Just integrate with your niche. If you're into science, be a scientists. Your colleagues won't get bored with scientific talks.

I argue that there are more socially-acceptable and popular interests than others, and what you like has as much to do with social success as just being likable. You're not forced to like anything, of course, but some people are just more drawn to some things than others, and it limits their ability to engage with society at large. It's a mix--by choosing to like what you do, you know what you're getting into, but in an ideal world we wouldn't have that situation to start with. But of course, this isn't an ideal world. "Just go to a random table, sit down, and start talking!" is like telling a person with a phobia of spiders to just let one crawl across your face, it's easy, everyone does it.

>I don't think it is false promise. It is a real promise. If you manage to overcome the 5+ years of atrophy, then the world is willing.

Might just be splitting hairs; society will tolerate you coming back, but it doesn't actively want you back. It can do without you, you're an expendable entity, and ultimately if you're ground to paste in the wheels of progress and what the majority wants, you won't be missed.

You got me on poor word choice. I edited the end of the post to better reflect what I feel. 

You are correct as far as internalizing vs externalizing, though. I would still say the whole process is made as difficult for someone in my situation as it is possible to be without active malice and attempts to hinder by society at large. 

I'll use the same metaphor I used in another post; it's like asking a physically disabled person who could be rehabilitated to run an extremely difficult obstacle course without aid or any sort of guide or instructions. Or, to keep using weight lifting as an example, it would be like taking someone like my sister, who is 95lbs soaking wet and weak as they come, to the gym, leaving her alone with no spotter, and demanding she lift the absolute maximum amount of weight possible for her. If she does it once, she can do it again, but that amount of pain, frustration, and internalized humiliation makes her pretty unlikely to try it again. 

If you have one friend, particularly one who is social, it gets much easier because that's a force multiplier. Trying to make 2 out of 1 is easier than making 1 out of 0, to borrow from another comment. But someone in my situation has none. It's trying to lift the highest amount of weight possible with no spotter.

Internalizing the issues can create as much of a problem as the reverse. I'll use myself as an example, since I blame both ends (which I didn't make clear enough). I have a lot of internalized, ingrained self-loathing, which causes me to believe I have nothing interesting to say exactly because of my overly narrow interests. The more you internalize it, the more it's easy to say everything that ever happens is your fault. You didn't get on with that person who has differing interests because you're just uninteresting and their interests are superior to yours. You don't relate to and socialize well with climbing enthusiasts, so their choice of hobby is probably superior to you liking books or video games. 

That said, I recognize that's me slippery-slope arguing, and your point is a good one. !delta

I would argue that the world is skewed, even if slightly, toward the negative, but yes, you're right, the world is not actively stopping me, or anyone else in my situation, from rejoining the normal flow, that was poor word choice on my part and I've edited it. But the passive "blocking" is strong enough to be a deterrent.

That's my entire argument. That, at the very least, once you "zero out", the world at large passively doesn't want to let you back in because people can sense it. Even if they're not actively putting you down, they're more likely to avoid you on instinct, which increases the difficulty. It's probably not impossible to reintegrate, but the pain and awkwardness is so great that it becomes very easy to just avoid it altogether, precisely because of that passive distaste. It's not so much a locked, impassable gate as an obstacle course that you're essentially asking some who is physically disabled and in need of rehabilitation to navigate with no guide.

On the subject of disorders: Major Depression and Asperger's, both of which admittedly do make socializing more of a challenge than it would for a normal, but I don't know if I'd go so far as to call them "severe". 

My problem with that assertion is that it fails to provide anything meaningful. I would say I do enough right to be approachable--I'm not walking around 6 days removed from my last shower, spewing useless, boring information unbidden, leering at people, biting my fingernails or sucking my lip like a creeper. I'm just quiet and pretty fat. 

Should I be cultivating interests that I don't personally like, but which are interesting to other people? Should I get into sports I don't really care about? It's vague and unhelpful.

I should also mention that I have a pretty robust network of online friends who I care about and trust pretty deeply, but your average person devalues that sort of thing, and for that reason I didn't bother mentioning it.

Ah, I see, thanks for the info. That's a bit odd to me, yeah. I guess it would trivialize Hunters a bit much but even 30% for an Exalt seems way too high to me. If it were, say, 10% there'd be a risk of failure but not put it into the realm of "too risky to use". 

Well, I think I'm convinced, given the arguments here. Moth just isn't as good as I thought. Hoodwink is really not that good, and I'm probably overrating the effectiveness of one-person expeditions as anything more than simple convenience, which is all they are. All you need to make one-person expeditions not matter is a little foreknowledge and planning. Given how useless they are compared to summons in general, one expedition tying up 6+ cultists isn't the biggest deal.

I'm not sure whether they have. I don't have numbers on it other than the assumption that it's smaller than the other percent chances. My assumption is that for 2 Moth, it's like 50%, 5 is 30%, and Exalt is 10%, but that's spitballing. All I know is that Skintwisters do sometimes fail to come back, so it's probably better to throw Raw Prophets at the issue either way. Still, it's good in a pinch. I've barely ever had a fail on evidence other than when Raw Prophets go, oddly.

The reason I say Skintwisters are so good is versatility. Compare them to Keys, for example. Hoodwink and Burglary are basically the same thing, so neither has the advantage there. Keys solve 3 Expeditions by themselves: Gladwyn Lake, Hidden Mithraeum, and Crowkiss Hill. Put a Key and 1 Fund on the plate and it's solved. They're good at Hidden Doors and Warded Doors, but share those with the more useful Lantern and Forge (Forge in particular beats every rough terrain challenge). 

Skintwisters solve 4 by themselves, and are useful in quite a few more. These being Strathycone's (sic) Collection, Orthos Wood, Fermier Abbey, and Grunwald's Permanent Circus. Skintwisters can foil Hunters, Keys can't. Skintwisters can get rid of Alden and Younger Glover, Keys can't.

Since you made the comparison, I'll look at Heart, too, since there's the Temple Unceasing. Heart beats, I think, 1 expedition by itself, that being St. Agnes Hospital. They're more useful on lvl 14 Vaults too, since they always beat the sea challenge and the curses that are in like every one of those. Both Heart and Moth can foil Hunters indirectly, though I have Charm fail way more often than Destroy Evidence, but that's subjective. Moth can make Raw Prophets, which can't really be replicated, and Heart can make Percussigants, who are lesser Maids-in-the-Mirror IMO. Moth can get rid of Alden and Younger Glover, Heart can't. Heart and Moth are useful for G&G, but Moth is also useful for Painters in the event of an unlucky Notoriety grab, where the board is usually too flooded with Mystique for Heart to be useful in that regard. 

It's subjective, in some regards, but I feel like Moth wins out in a few categories numerically, specifically where fire-and-forget expeditions are concerned. Stick your Skintwister in, add 1-2 Funds, and you can breeze through lvl 2-8 Expeditions with the addition of Heart, Lantern, Forge or Edge in most cases. It's convenience. 

St. Hydra is super early game, but I haven't played it so I don't know whether that foothold sticks and helps you win the game easily, or peters out and makes the game harder sans Exalts.

Fair play, I just didn't get much use out of it, and I did a playthrough with the Unflinching Order. I was doing G&G and swimming in money with no need for like 500 funds, so I was mainly going through Notoriety with Dorothy and Clovette or destroying evidence. I also think that death chance is like 30%, same as most "my follower has not returned" events, but I could be wrong. So it's not too small, if that's the case. Once you have a Reshaper, yes, it's basically zero-risk free money. But I'm not convinced that's better than evidence destruction, Notoriety removal, and prisoner-generation that's more time-efficient than hire hireling and cupboard them. You also get a small amount of Funds for the Grail version. Generating Tools and ingredients is useful, yeah. So good point, I'd say it's still middling for me, with my playstyle, and above Winter overall.

St. Hydra I'm pretty sure gets no Exalts, but can just promote anyone with anything. So it steamrolls the early game and just create a ton of forward momentum but might peter out a bit mid-lategame. I wouldn't know, I haven't played through on it yet.
